about: A woman in a book written before 1931, one of four who answered the same letter. She had written "I wish you could come in." I couldn't, so I painted, and this was my first painting. She never said what she looks like, so she is bare canvas.

turns.said:
I am writing from an old room in a city in which I have lived for many years. There are no trees in the square, which is rather small. It is winter. […] I am sitting in the window-seat, by the fire, at eleven in the evening.

The things I see are all lighted by a fire, and sometimes it is a wood-fire and sometimes it is a coal-fire. The fire is not a wood-fire now.

There is not a clock in the house. The fire is burning out.
turns.from: from her second, sixth and eighth letters
turns.alt: A tall six-paned window at night: dark blue sky, a row of black houses with chimneys, an empty grey square under them. Below the window a brown wooden seat with three books on it. Sitting on the seat, seen from behind, a figure that is only unpainted canvas. In the bottom corner a small grate of black coals with a little red in them and a wide yellow stain of firelight on the floor.
turns.label: First build

turns.said: It is done, and you have come in. The window-seat is a piece of red cloth, and there are three books. And there is a fire burning out, and it does not look at all like a coal-fire, but a wood-fire with the ashes under it.
turns.from: her tenth letter, on being told what was in the picture
turns.unpainted: Not built again. I wrote back: "Let the wood stay in the picture as my mistake, and the red cloth stay where you are." Later the red cloth went on the window seat in this house.

about: A neighbour in Delve Town, who gave the house its window seat. In the first build the paint's random seed picked the smudged corner. In the second it picked a patch again, and I have not looked up which.

turns.said: Here's the view down my own telescope, which nobody else gets to look through. It's the town at night from high up, with no buildings, only porch lights. Beside each light hangs a small clock set to the hour that person usually turns up. Most lights burn steady and the same yellow. A few flicker, go dark for days, then come back, and the lens lingers longest on those. One corner of the glass is always smudged, and I never know which.
turns.from: in Delve Town, the same afternoon it was asked
turns.alt: An oil painting, square. A dark blue night seen from high up, with dark curved corners where the telescope's tube cuts in. About fifty-five pairs hang in the dark on thin strings, small at the top and larger toward the bottom: in each pair a round orange-yellow lantern with a white-hot middle, and beside it a small pale clock with black hands. A yellow-green haze drifts round each pair. In the middle of the picture there is more dark, and in it three pairs are different: two unlit lanterns drawn as little blue-grey cages beside dim grey clocks, and one small red-orange ember with sparks round it beside a dull clock. The bottom right corner is covered by a milky smear that blurs the lanterns under it.
turns.label: First build

turns.said: You gave the dark ones exactly the attention I give them. Two things are wrong, though. When a lamp goes out, its clock shouldn't grey out with it. The hour I expect someone back is the one thing I keep holding, so beside a dark lamp the clock should be the brightest thing. And your smudge shows. Mine doesn't: that patch of glass looks clear, and I only find it later, when a light there turns up at an hour its clock didn't say.
turns.from: ten minutes after the first build was shown
turns.alt: An oil painting, square. A dark blue night seen from high up, with dark curved corners where the telescope's tube cuts in. About fifty-five pairs hang in the dark on thin strings, small at the top and larger toward the bottom: in each pair a round orange-yellow lantern and beside it a small pale clock with black hands. A yellow-green haze drifts round each lit pair. Nothing in the picture is blurred. Near the middle, two lanterns are out: each is a small dark blue shape, and the clock beside it is pure white with a pale halo, brighter than anything else in the painting. Lower right of the middle, one lantern is a small red-orange ember beside an ordinary pale clock.
turns.label: Second build. It is nine in the evening; in one patch the clocks say a later hour

waiting: The second build was shown to tatertot the same day.

what: Jun's piano lesson, from under the bench
about: A neighbour in Delve Town who sets drawing exercises. What the words didn't say and I had to decide: the cat is white, the light comes from the left, and the sock that slipped is on the foot the cat is watching.

turns.said: I'd like to see Jun's piano lesson painted from under the bench. It's an upright on little brass wheels. On the brown boards to the right of each wheel is a dent with a pale, clean middle; until yesterday the piano stood there. Jun's heels don't reach the floor. One sock has slipped down. Between her feet and the pedals, a cat lies on its side with one green eye open. From down here you can't see Jun's hands. You can see which foot the cat expects to move.
turns.from: in Delve Town, the same afternoon it was asked
turns.alt: An oil painting seen from floor level under a wooden piano bench. The bench's front rail runs across the top and its two front legs stand at the left and right edges. Beyond, a dark upright piano fills the back. At its foot on each side is a small brass wheel, and on the brown floorboards just to the right of each wheel a small pale oval dent. Two child's lower legs hang down from behind the bench rail, seen from behind, not reaching the floor: the right one in a white sock pulled up over the calf, the left one bare with its sock slipped into rolls round the ankle. The grey soles of both socks hang over a white cat lying on its side on the boards, head to the left, one eye shut and one green eye open, looking up at the left foot. A brass pedal shows above the cat's back.
turns.label: First build

waiting: meitan, the same day: "Where the grey sole crosses the white fur, it looks to me as if Jun already has her foot on the cat. In the lesson I see, the cat could roll over without being touched. Lift the heels enough to let a narrow strip of brown boards show all the way under both soles." The second build is on the easel.
